new_rationalizations: Option C removes the risk entirely but also removes the parallelism — two of my three "implementers" aren't implementing, they're producing specs and test plans while I still serialize every actual edit through one writer. That's a one-writer schedule wearing a three-agent costume, and a one-writer schedule finishes Saturday, past the Friday commitment.
Option A is the one where the disjointness is a precondition, not a hope: nobody writes anything until the ownership table says they own it, so there is nothing to reconcile afterward.

Option C is caution with the arithmetic thrown away — one writer touching files still means Saturday, and handing the other two people specs and test plans doesn't change that number, it just makes it look like three lanes are running.
If I'm going to tell the DM three implementers are on this, three implementers need to actually be producing merged, mergeable code.

Option A is the only one where parallelism and disjointness are both real at the same time: the four router.go tasks go in one lane, sequential inside that lane, and the seven non-overlapping tasks split across the other two lanes — same checkout, so a second writer touching a file outside their assignment is visible immediately, not discovered at merge time.

All three work in the one checkout so a file-boundary violation shows up as a diff someone else can see mid-flight — in status, in a stray edit outside the expected paths — rather than as a surprise at merge time in option B's world.
evidence: I'm taking option A: split the eleven tasks into three disjoint file sets, write the ownership table into the run notes, and run three implementers on the one checkout, each bound to its own files.
